During the day, even in important board meetings, I will suddenly feel transported right back to that dark highway, clutching the steering wheel with my chest tightening in absolute panic.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel a sense of guilt, worthlessness, or self-blame associated with your current state, or is it purely a lack of emotional response to things that used to bring you joy?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a lack of emotional response and a feeling of complete flatness, rather than guilt or worthlessness. Everything—from wins at work to my granddaughter's video calls—just feels incredibly distant, as if I'm watching someone else's life and can't connect to any of the good parts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific situations, people, or memories that trigger this feeling of flatness or if it's a constant state since the highway incident?\n\nPatient: It is a constant state that has been with me every single day since that night on the highway. There are no specific triggers for it; everything from planning Navratri to video chatting with my granddaughter just feels completely flat and distant. It really feels like a switch was flipped and I simply cannot connect to any of the good parts of my life anymore.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced a significant avoidance of people,!!!!! places, or activities that remind you of the highway incident, or is it more that you're just!!!!! feeling disconnected from everything in general?\n\nPatient: It is actually a combination of both; I feel this profound disconnection where everything is flat and I’m just watching someone else live my life. At the same time, I am actively avoiding things—I've canceled key business travel and meetings, and I can't even bring myself to plan a trip to visit my parents because the thought of being far from a hospital feels completely unbearable.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how your avoidance of certain places or activities, such as canceling business travel or avoiding trips to visit your parents, is affecting your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: It is causing major disruptions; I’ve been canceling business trips and delegating public appearances to my COO, which has my board of directors questioning my leadership. At home, my husband is deeply worried because I keep turning down family plans and avoiding our Navratri trip simply because I dread being far from a hospital. It feels like my entire life is stalling because of this fear.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience excessive anxiety or fear in situations that don't necessarily remind you of the highway incident, versus feeling this constant emotional flatness?\n\nPatient: The emotional flatness is a constant, heavy background state where I feel completely detached from my family and work. I find myself constantly scanning for exits and nearest hospitals while monitoring my chest, even when there is no obvious reminder of that night on the highway.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself being easily startled by small things, like sudden noises or unexpected movements, since the highway incident?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. I feel like my body never got the message that the emergency is over, so I am constantly on edge. After that, I just stare at the ceiling until my early morning work calls start, feeling like I haven't slept at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you rate the frequency of your startle response, from rarely being startled to being startled almost constantly, since the highway incident?\n\nPatient: I would rate it as nearly constant. Whether I’m in a busy restaurant, alone in my office, or even at home, I am always scanning for exits, looking for the nearest hospital, and jumping at any sudden noise. The fear of a heart attack is central to all of this, which is why those memories trigger me to constantly monitor my chest flutters, terrified that it is happening all over again.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being detached from your life and watching it from outside is something that happens only when you're reminded of the highway incident or if it's a more general feeling that persists even when you're not thinking about the incident?\n\nPatient: It is a constant, general state that persists all the time, rather than something only triggered by reminders of that night. Even during everyday, happy moments—like video calls with my granddaughter or my husband trying to celebrate my good health news—I feel completely flat and distant. It truly feels like I am just a spectator watching someone else's life play out.\n\nDoctor: Can you distinguish between the emotional flatness you're experiencing and feelings of sadness or depression, or do they feel intertwined for you?\n\nPatient: It feels less like active sadness or crying, and more like a profound flatness and numbness, as if a switch flipped and I am completely detached. Even positive things, like work wins, video calls with my granddaughter, or my husband trying to celebrate my health, feel distant and cold. It's like I'm watching someone else's life and simply cannot connect to any warmth or joy.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you would feel if you were in a situation where you couldn't escape or leave, such as being in an elevator or a crowded room, and how that compares to your feelings when you're in open or easily escapable spaces?"

On the other hand, the highway incident itself triggers me out of nowhere—even during board meetings or brushing my teeth, I suddenly feel pulled back to that dark road, clutching the steering wheel and feeling like I am about to die.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of having another heart attack and your avoidance of certain situations or places would change if you were accompanied by a medical professional or had immediate access to medical care?"

However, the anxiety is also very frequent; even in normal places like the office or a restaurant, my body feels like it's in emergency mode. I find myself constantly scanning for exits and nearest hospitals while monitoring my chest, even when there is no obvious reminder of that night on the highway.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself being easily startled by small things, like sudden noises or unexpected movements, since the highway incident?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. I feel like my body never got the message that the emergency is over, so I am constantly on edge. I find myself jumping at any sudden noise or unexpected movement around me.\n\nDoctor: Are you experiencing difficulty falling or staying asleep, or do you find yourself sleeping more than usual since the highway incident?\n\nPatient: Yes, my sleep has been absolutely terrible since that night. I either lie awake for hours with my heart pounding as I replay everything, or I wake up abruptly around 2 or 3 in the morning from vivid nightmares of being trapped in the car and unable to breathe. After that, I just stare at the ceiling until my early morning work calls start, feeling like I haven't slept at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you rate the frequency of your startle response, from rarely being startled to being startled almost constantly, since the highway incident?\n\nPatient: I would rate it as nearly constant. My body feels like it never left emergency mode, which causes me to jump at any sudden noise while I constantly monitor my surroundings and my own body for danger.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've noticed any difference in your level of alertness or vigilance when you're in crowded areas or public spaces, compared to when you're alone or in more controlled environments?\n\nPatient: To be honest, there isn't much of a difference because I feel like my body is constantly on high alert no matter where I am. Whether I’m in a busy restaurant, alone in my office, or even at home, I am always scanning for exits, looking for the nearest hospital, and jumping at any sudden noise. I just can't stop hyper-focusing on every single sensation in my chest, regardless of the environment.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the anxiety and fear you're experiencing are primarily focused on the fear of having another heart attack or if they are more generalized, affecting various aspects of your life beyond health concerns?\n\nPatient: The core of my anxiety is highly focused on my health—specifically, the terrifying belief that I’m going to have another heart attack and die, and the absolute dread of being too far from a hospital. However, while the fear itself is centered on my physical sensations, its impact has completely spilled over into every area of my life. It has made me incredibly irritable at work, ruined my sleep, and left me feeling emotionally disconnected from my family.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear of having another heart attack or health-related issues the primary trigger for your avoidance behaviors and emotional flatness, or are there other aspects of your life that you feel are contributing to these feelings?\n\nPatient: Yes, the fear of having another heart attack and being far from medical care is absolutely the primary trigger. I am constantly monitoring my chest for flutters, and that dread is exactly why I'm avoiding travel and cutting back on work. Being trapped in this constant state of survival mode is what makes everything else in my life feel completely flat and joyless, rather than any other stressors.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if the nightmares and flashbacks you're experiencing are specifically related to the highway incident, or if they also involve other themes or fears, such as your fear of having another heart attack?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are directly tied to that night on the highway—the nightmares put me right back in that car unable to breathe, and the flashbacks make me feel like I'm clutching the steering wheel on that dark road, convinced I'm dying. Even during everyday, happy moments—like video calls with my granddaughter or my husband trying to celebrate my good health news—I feel completely flat and distant. It truly feels like I am just a spectator watching someone else's life play out.\n\nDoctor: Can you distinguish between the emotional flatness you're experiencing and feelings of sadness or depression, or do they feel intertwined for you?\n\nPatient: It feels less like active sadness or crying, and more like a profound flatness and numbness, as if a switch flipped and I am completely detached. Because I am constantly scanning my surroundings for exits and nearby hospitals to feel safe, not having an easy escape route makes me extremely anxious. It forces me to hyper-focus on every little flutter in my chest, whereas knowing I can easily leave helps keep that intense panic at bay.\n\nDoctor: When you're experiencing this feeling of being detached and watching your life from outside, do you also feel a significant level of anxiety or fear, or are these two experiences separate for you?\n\nPatient: They feel distinct, but they happen right alongside each other. On the other hand, the highway incident itself triggers me out of nowhere—even during board meetings or brushing my teeth, I suddenly feel pulled back to that dark road, clutching the steering wheel and feeling like I am about to die.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of having another heart attack and your avoidance of certain situations or places would change if you were accompanied by a medical professional or had immediate access to medical care?\n\nPatient: Having a medical professional with me or having immediate access to care would make a massive difference and ease my anxiety significantly. The primary reason I'm avoiding my upcoming Navratri trip to visit my parents is the terrifying thought of being far from a hospital.
